title: Pride And Prejudice: CHAPTER LIX
enhanced_title: The Revelation of Elizabeth's Engagement - Chapter 59 of Pride and Prejudice: A Study in Transformation and Familial Acceptance
author: Jane Austen
description: Chapter 59 chronicles Elizabeth Bennet's revelation of her engagement to Mr. Darcy, her sister Jane's incredulous joy, and the difficult process of securing parental consent. The chapter explores the transformation of Darcy from a detested figure to a beloved son-in-law, Elizabeth's internal struggle with her former prejudices, and the comedic contrast between Mr. Bennet's thoughtful consideration and Mrs. Bennet's mercenary enthusiasm.

analysis_entries.paragraph: This opening scene establishes the atmosphere of secret knowledge and the contrast between acknowledged and unacknowledged lovers. Elizabeth's confusion and embarrassment create dramatic tension, while her internal concerns about her family's reaction to Darcy foreshadow the challenges ahead. The subtle psychological portrait here reveals that Elizabeth's understanding of her family's prejudices mirrors her own former attitude toward Darcy, as she was aware that no one liked him but Jane; and even feared that with the others it was a dislike which not all his fortune and consequence might do away.
analysis_entries.anchor_text_end_of_sentence:
she was aware that no one
liked him but Jane; and even feared that with the others it was a
_dislike_ which not all his fortune and consequence might do away.

analysis_entries.paragraph: The disclosure to Jane represents a pivotal moment of sisterly intimacy and dramatic irony. Jane's absolute incredulity underscores how completely Elizabeth's former hatred of Darcy was known and how unexpected this reversal appears. Elizabeth's declaration that 'a good memory is unpardonable' in such cases reveals the profound transformation in her character and the theme that love can overcome initial prejudice, as she vows that this is the last time she shall ever remember it herself.
analysis_entries.anchor_text_end_of_sentence:
This is the last time I shall ever
remember it myself.

analysis_entries.paragraph: Jane's concern about Elizabeth's true feelings introduces an important theme of authentic affection versus practical considerations in marriage. Elizabeth's confession that she loves Darcy better than Bingley carries significant weight, as Bingley was previously presented as the ideal marital prospect. The dating of her love from first seeing Pemberley's grounds is richly symbolic, representing how appreciation of Darcy's true character and estate became intertwined with her growing affection.
analysis_entries.anchor_text_end_of_sentence:
but I believe I must date it from my first seeing his beautiful grounds
at Pemberley.

analysis_entries.paragraph: Mrs. Bennet's ignorant hostility toward Darcy provides comic relief while highlighting the dramatic irony of the situation. Her continued use of the epithet 'disagreeable' and her desire that Darcy go 'a-shooting' rather than visit demonstrates how completely she misunderstands the man who will become her son-in-law. Elizabeth's vexation and ironic amusement reveal her position between two worlds—her former prejudices and her present happiness—as she could hardly help laughing at so convenient a proposal.
analysis_entries.anchor_text_end_of_sentence:
Elizabeth could hardly help laughing at so convenient a proposal; yet
was really vexed that her mother should be always giving him such an
epithet.

analysis_entries.paragraph: Mr. Bennet's conversation with Elizabeth presents the most serious exploration of marriage and happiness in the chapter. His initial opposition based on Elizabeth's former hatred of Darcy reveals his genuine concern for her welfare rather than any mercenary calculation. The father's advice reflects Austen's serious consideration of what makes a successful marriage, warning against the dangers of an unequal union where respect is lacking, and urging Elizabeth not to let him have the grief of seeing her unable to respect her partner in life.
analysis_entries.anchor_text_end_of_sentence:
My child, let me not have the grief of seeing
_you_ unable to respect your partner in life.

analysis_entries.paragraph: Elizabeth's revelation of Darcy's role in Lydia's marriage transforms Mr. Bennet's understanding entirely. The father's astonishment and subsequent qualified approval demonstrate how Darcy's actions speak louder than his reserved demeanor. This disclosure serves as the final piece of evidence that convinces Mr. Bennet of Darcy's worthiness, and his conclusion—'If this be the case, he deserves you'—shows that moral action and generosity of spirit overcome proud reserve in establishing character.
analysis_entries.anchor_text_end_of_sentence:
I could not have parted with
you, my Lizzy, to anyone less worthy.

analysis_entries.paragraph: Mrs. Bennet's reaction provides the chapter's comedic climax and social commentary. Her immediate translation of the engagement into material terms—pin-money, jewels, carriages, ten thousand a year—reveals her mercenary priorities. The contrast between her stunned silence and subsequent effusion demonstrates how completely she operates within a world of financial calculation rather than emotional understanding. Her sudden affection for the 'charming man' represents the ultimate social transformation of Darcy's reputation.

summary: Chapter 59 of Pride and Prejudice masterfully depicts the aftermath of Elizabeth Bennet's engagement to Mr. Darcy, focusing on the gradual revelation to family members and the transformation of perceptions. The chapter is structured around three key disclosures: first to Jane, whose incredulous joy gives way to delighted acceptance; then to Mr. Bennet, whose serious concerns about Elizabeth's happiness are only overcome when he learns of Darcy's essential goodness and his role in saving Lydia; and finally to Mrs. Bennet, whose volte-face from hostility to mercenary enthusiasm provides comic relief. Throughout, Austen explores themes of prejudice and transformation, the true foundations of marital happiness, and the contrast between genuine attachment and materialistic calculation. The chapter demonstrates Elizabeth's own growth as she confronts her former opinions and the social consequences of her choice, while Darcy's character is rehabilitated through action rather than words.
